title: Built on SAP Digital Manufacturing: A new view of the Product History Report
author: ManoelCosta
text:
If you work with SAP Digital Manufacturing, you know the Product History Report. It is the full record of how one unit was built. Every operation, every measurement, every nonconformance, every component that went into it, with its serial or lot or batch. 
 It is also several pages long, full of tables and data. 
 That is fine when you need the legal record. It is not fine when you are standing on the floor trying to answer a simple question: is this part good, and did anything go wrong while we built it. 
 So I built a small tool to fix that one thing.

title: Sharing Capabilities, Not Data. From Data Mesh to Agent Mesh.
author: Julia_Gudelius
text:
How a Large Enterprise organizes Agents by the Principles of the Data Mesh 

 Reviewer: @Rene_de_Daniel , Axel Schwarz, @Stefan_Fassmann , Kay Jeschke 
 Motivation: The rapid growth of AI agents and skills, which are often made available through forums or shared platforms without clearly defined ownership, has highlighted an important challenge. In many cases, these individual products are not consistently updated, maintained, or governed over time. 
 This has led us to reflect on proven approaches from data management and to explore whether the democratization of data could also be applied to AI agents and capabilities. We are considering whether similar principles, such as domain ownership, data products, self-service enablement, and governance, can be transferred to the AI domain. 
 The goal would be to enable a decentralized management model for AI capabilities, like what has been established for data. This approach could help ensure clearer responsibilities, better maintainability, improved discoverability, and more consistent governance across AI agents and skills. 

 1 Building an Agent Mesh 
 An Agent Mesh gives AI agents what they currently lack: clear ownership, maintenance and governance, organized by the principles of the Data Mesh. 
 A Data Mesh distributes the responsibility for analytical data to the business domains in which the data originates, instead of handing the data over to a central data warehouse or data lake. Each domain provides it as a product.[ 1,2] The Data Mesh has shown how a large enterprise gets a grip on data that is created across dozens of domains: through domain ownership, product thinking, a self-serve platform and federated governance.[1,2] An Agent Mesh transfers these four principles to agents, and keeps the three levels on which the Data Mesh is described: the strategic level (where an agent belongs), the actor level (who is accountable for it) and the technical level (what it runs on). 
 The principles are vendor-neutral. We illustrate them using the example of a large SAP enterprise, because SAP’s reference architecture already describes processes down to the individual business activity. Other landscapes need an equivalent process model. Figure 1 shows the structure. Alexander Thamm, McKinsey and SAP arrive at this structure independently of one another: agents as products with ownership and lifecycle,[3] domain ownership separated from a central platform and guardrails,[4] “Agents are organized by business domain, not by individual systems”.[ 5] 

 Fig. 1: Building an Agent Mesh – four principles, three levels; the Data Mesh as foundation. 
 1.1 Domain Ownership (Data Mesh: Domain Ownership) 
 Strategic: placement in the reference architecture. An agent belongs to a business capability and thereby to an end-to-end process, not to an application. For an SAP enterprise the place is already mapped out. The SAP Reference Business Architecture (RBA) describes all business capabilities and all processes down to the business activity, the individual process step. The SAP Reference Solution Architecture (RSA) describes what realizes these capabilities.[6] So far, these have been applications . An Agent Mesh adds a second form of realization. A business capability is now also fulfilled by agents. The agent is anchored to the business capability and the application that realizes it, as well as to the business activities (process step) it performs or supports. It is documented in SAP LeanIX, in detail in the SAP AI Agent Hub (Fig. 2). 

 Fig. 2: LeanIX placement of assistants, agents and features in RBA/RSA – processes down to the business activity, capabilities down to level 3; the agent realizes a capability like an application. Solution side omitted. 
 This introduces a consequence with no equivalent in Data Mesh, the potential impact can be measured after the agent has been built. Because every process step is already described, the intended effect of the agent can be recorded per business activity (for example cycle time, error rate, escalation frequency) and measured later against the actual value. SAP Signavio provides Process Mining for this, which checks whether an agent “is following the execution pathway it was built for”, and ties agent quality to the KPIs of the process.[5] 
 Actor: process owners as agent owners. The business unit that is accountable for the process defines the goal, the context and the decision boundaries of its agents.[ 7] Whoever owns the process owns the agent, not IT, and not a central AI team. 
 Technical: process twin. The agent runs on the shared platform (Section 1.3) but works through MCP and APIs against the system of record of its own domain; it reaches other domains through their agents, not through their data.[5] The guiding structure is the process, as a definition down to the business activity or as a digital twin.[3] 
 SAP Example: Domain Owner for “Autonomous Finance - Cash and Treasury Assistant” has deployed the SAP Agent “SAP Cash Positioning Agent” for the Process Variant “Manage payment, cash and risk (public sector) / Manage cash and working capital” and the Business Capability “Finance / Treasury Management / Cash and Liquidity Management” 
 1.2 Agents as Products (Data Mesh: Data as a Product) 
 Strategic: product, not project. An agent has an owner, a version, a maturity level and a lifecycle that ends with decommissioning. It is not a temporary IT artifact but a lasting enterprise capability.[ 7] Its users, people as well as other agents, are treated as customers. 
 Actor: the agent catalog. The domain team publishes its agent in a catalog that plays the same role for agents as the data catalog plays for data products, extended by what only agents have, permitted actions, target processes and known risks.[7] An agent goes live only once this entry has been verified. In SAP’s software stack the SAP AI Agent Hub in SAP LeanIX takes on this task; it is at the same time the marketplace in which agents are published with standardized metadata, quality metrics and trust ratings.[ 5] 
 Technical: interfaces with meaning. The agent exposes an A2A endpoint with an agent card and is described in SAP LeanIX as an application with the subtype AI Agent; it connects its tools through MCP. A2A and MCP are the preferred standards for SAP for multi-agent collaboration and tool connectivity.[5] Like applications, SAP’s own Agents descriptions are provided with the SAP Reference Architecture content in LeanIX. They can be imported into the inventory together with the required applications and the provided business capabilities.[ 8] The agents from the reference content provide important information, e.g. what the agent delivers, which preconditions apply and which effects it triggers.[7] 
 SAP Example: SAP Agent “SAP Cash Positioning Agent” is provisioned in SAP for Me Managed in LeanIX and enables the Application “SAP S/4HANA Cloud Private Edition”. It ensures that bank statements are processed accurately, aggregates opening balances, and accounts for expected cash flows. 
 SAP will provide lifecycle management support for SAP agents. 
 1.3 Self-Serve Agent Platform (Data Mesh: Self-serve Data Platform) 
 Strategic: a domain-independent catalog. Identity, observability and evaluation come from the platform, not from the individual agent. SAP puts it in one formula: “The model reasons. The harness governs.”[ 5] For the domains this means they build agents, not operating infrastructure. 
 Actor: a central platform team with the right to enforce. One team operates the runtime, the gateway, the registry and pre-approved build paths. It sits with the enterprise architecture function and is supported by the agent stewards who are accountable in the domains. 
 Technical: SAP AI Agent Hub, Joule Studio, SAP Business AI Platform. An agent and tool gateway handles authentication, principal propagation and policy enforcement; a skills registry makes building blocks reusable; sandbox and evaluations are built in.[5] 
 SAP Example: The Agents which are deployed are discoverable in LeanIX. The Agent Owner is named in the fact sheet. 
 1.4 Federated Governance (Data Mesh: Federated Governance) 
 Strategic: ontology and integration contracts. For agents to collaborate across domain boundaries they need a shared language: the enterprise ontology or knowledge graph that the enterprise has to build itself.[ 7] The process model of the RBA depicts how the applications involved in a process work together and defines the communication between the individual business activities (tasks). The gateway draws the landscape boundaries within which an agent may access systems.[ 5] 
 Actor: an agentic governance board. Domain owners, the platform and risk and compliance jointly set the standards and are accountable for agent approvals. Liability stays with people, “Responsibility cannot be delegated.”[ 5] 
 Technical: governance as code at runtime. Rules, roles, rights, approval thresholds and escalation paths are machine-readable policies in the system,[ 7] enforced at the point of execution.[ 9] Verified agents and MCP servers automatically lose access when their status changes.[ 10] Tracing captures every tool call. 
 SAP Example: The risk classification applies to internal use of AI and to AI in products. High-risk systems are subject to ongoing monitoring, human oversight and controls relating to data and accuracy. Third-party components undergo due diligence and ongoing audits. SAP adheres to ISO and NIST standards and provides customers with the documentation they need to meet their own compliance obligations. The EU AI Act and the US AI Action Plan are regulatory drivers.[ 5] 
 1.5 What Is New Compared with the Data Mesh: Agents Act 
 Three things carry over without loss: the ownership question, the product idea and the compounding effect of reused capabilities.[ 7] New is a property that no data product has, an agent acts. From this follows a third governance level above data governance and AI governance, which Thamm calls agentic governance “Agentic Governance governs action.”[3] This means three things for the architecture: 
 Agent identity: the agent is a principal in its own right “agents are first-class principals, they authenticate, receive authorizations, and are governed like any other enterprise actor” to which users can delegate only “a bounded subset of their permissions”.[ 5] 
 Decision boundaries instead of quality SLAs: an agent product has to state what it may execute, when it escalates and what a rollback looks like. 
 Evaluation of the whole chain instead of input-output tests including context and policy boundaries, continuously in operation.[ 7] 
 SAP Example: The agent's identity is governed by the role and authorization concepts of the underlying applications. 
 1.6 Sharing Capabilities, Not Data 
 The decisive difference for the enterprise is economic. A data product is the value it shares, whoever receives it has the data. An agent product shares capability, dispute resolution, skill matching while access to the data stays with the data product and its authorizations. SAP builds on exactly this separation. Data products are “the primary governed interface between SAP data and everything that wants to use it, whether it is a dashboard, a data science platform, an application, a human or an AI agent.”[5] An agent can therefore be passed on, reused and published in the marketplace without trade secrets leaving the data perimeter. Provided data governance remains the innermost layer (Fig. 1, bottom). 
 Two caveats apply: 
 The separation holds for the interface, not automatically for the runtime. Agents move data across system boundaries and leave it behind in prompts and caches.[ 11] The perimeter only holds if the platform enforces tenant separation and context filtering, a claim SAP makes for its platform.[ 5] 
 And the asset worth protecting shifts. Prompts, instructions, tool definitions and

title: New Version of the SAP Warehouse Logistics Mobile App
author: NadineRied
text:
What's New in the SAP Warehouse Logistics Mobile App 
 We are excited to announce the latest release of the SAP Warehouse Logistics mobile app - packed with new capabilities designed to streamline warehouse operations and make the daily work of warehouse operatives faster and more efficient. 

 Picking with Picking Handling Units 
 Picking into picking handling units is now fully supported on the mobile app. Operatives can execute picking processes directly with picking handling units, enabling a more structured and traceable approach to outbound logistics. This is especially valuable in warehouses that work with pallets or consolidated containers during the picking process - reducing errors and improving throughput. 
 This completes the earlier shipped features for the desktop applications. For more information on the outbound process with picking handling units, please have a look at this blog post . 
 For now, let's focus on the new capabilities in the mobile app. Here is how the process on the mobile app looks with the new app release: 
 Once the warehouse operative started a picking warehouse task for an outbound process there is an option to confirm the picked products into an earlier created picking handling unit (note: picking handling units can be created in the Manage Handling Units App : 

 The warehouse operative either scans or manually enters the picking handling unit number as defined in the verification profiles and with this confirms the warehouse task. 
 In case the warehouse operative recently used a picking handling unit with the same destination storage bin as the current warehouse task, the system proposes this picking handling unit. The warehouse operative has the option to overwrite it. 

 Once the warehouse operative confirms the picking warehouse task, the system creates a drop off task for the picking handling unit to the destination storage bin which can be either confirmed directly or at a later point in time via the new Drop Off button at the bottom of the screen: 

 Scan EAN and GTIN Barcodes to Identify Products 
 Product verification just got easier. The app now supports scanning of EAN and GTIN barcodes, allowing warehouse operatives to quickly and accurately identify products without manual entry. By leveraging the mobile device's camera or a connected scanner, operatives can match products to warehouse tasks in seconds - minimizing mistakes and accelerating processing times 

 New Option During Warehouse Task Confirmation: No Stock 
 During warehouse task confirmation, the warehouse operative has now the possibility to record in case there is no stock at the requested storage bin: 

 Get Started 
 These new features are available with the latest version of the SAP Warehouse Logistics mobile app which can be found in the App Store and Google Playstore.

title: When Innovation Gets Tangible: Inside SAP's New Experience Garage AI Space
author: dora_kollar
text:
There's a question that anyone who cares about meaningful work eventually asks: how do you make innovation feel real ? 
 Not abstract. Not a slide deck. Not a link buried in a company intranet. Real – as in, you walk up to something, touch it, try it, and five minutes later you've built something you didn't think you could. 
 That's the question the SAP Experience Garage has been working on. And with its new Physical AI experience space at the SAP headquarters in Walldorf, it's found a compelling one. 
 What Is the SAP Experience Garage? 
 The SAP Experience Garage is SAP's platform for employee-led innovation. Through gamified learning, knowledge sharing, and peer-driven collaboration, it fosters a culture of exploration across SAP, where ideas aren't just pitched, but actively developed into impactful solutions. 
 At its core, it's built around one belief: innovation thrives when everyone can connect with the right tools. Whether you're a business strategist with a bold idea, a developer eager to take on a challenge, or a data scientist looking for fresh inspiration, the platform connects you with the people and resources to move forward. Cross-functional collaboration isn't a nice-to-have here, it's the whole point. 
 And it's working. With over 75,000 SAP employees on the platform, the Garage has been quietly driving a meaningful mindset shift: one where data and AI are no longer the domain of specialists, where experimentation is encouraged, and where faster problem-solving is within everyone's reach regardless of technical background. It's also a living expression of SAP runs SAP — using our own tools and AI capabilities to empower our own people first, and proving what's possible from the inside out. 
 The Garage space 
 The Platform Came First. The Place Comes NOW. 
 For all its strengths, digital has its limits. 
 No matter how well-designed a platform is, it can still feel distant from everyday work – something you'll explore eventually. Meanwhile, in-person experiences have the power to make a deeper, more lasting impression. As Niraj Singh, head of the SAP Experience Garage, puts it: “Doing it onsite. Hands-on. In the room. The moments between the sessions. The spontaneous debates. The energy you can’t schedule. Reconnecting with colleagues, friends, and meeting new ones. That kind of human exchange - unfiltered, unpredictable, real - is something no AI will ever replace.” 
 The physical Garage space recreates that dynamic by bringing innovation out of the screen and into the room: a dedicated space where AI isn't a concept to be studied, but an experience to be had. 
 This is not a showroom. It's not a demo center. It's a space built for doing. 
 Two Showcases. Two "Aha" Moments. 
 The Garage currently features two hands-on showcases in Walldorf, each designed to shift a mindset in a matter of minutes. 
 The App Machine makes vibe coding tangible. Instead of writing code, visitors use physical buttons and controllers to define the basic parameters of their app - creating its unique "DNA". They then describe what the app should do in a few simple sentences. No technical language or advanced prompting skills are required. Powered by Claude Code, a working prototype is generated in less than five minutes and can be tested directly on the station's touch-sensitive screen. The result is not only visible, but immediately interactive. 
 The App Machine turns an idea into a working, interactive app within minutes - making Al-powered software creation accessible, tangible, and intuitive for everyone, regardless of technical expertise. 
 The Game of Joule brings the impact of Al in everyday work to life through a competitive, hands-on experience. Across a simulated workweek, players face typical business tasks and decide when to handle them themselves and when to rely on Joule. Because Joule can only be used a limited number of times, every decision matters. The experience highlights where Al can create the greatest value by saving time, reducing effort, and supporting better, more efficient ways of working. 
 Game of Joule demonstrates that the real value of Al lies in using it where it makes the biggest difference - helping people work more efficiently and focus their time on higher-value tasks. 
 Together, these two showcases don't just demonstrate what SAP technology can do. They make it personal. The people who have already visited The Garage and tried our showcases echoed the same sentiment, highlighting the hands-on nature of the experience and how it doesn’t feel like a typical demo or enablement session. Others pointed to the conversations that were sparked among their team following the visit. The feedback is clear: in The Garage, you are not just a passive observer – you are an active participant in your own enablement. 
 Why This Matters Beyond SAP 
 A robot waving in front of The Garage The challenge of enabling people to act on innovation isn't unique to SAP. Every large organization wrestles with the same gap: the distance between a great idea and the confidence to pursue it. 
 Physical spaces that lower that barrier, that make experimentation feel safe, fast, and even fun, are increasingly rare and increasingly valuable. The Garage is a bet that the most powerful way to build a culture of innovation isn't to mandate it from the top, but to let people experience it for themselves. 
 When someone spends five minutes at The App Machine and walks away with something they built, that's not just a demo. That's a shift in how they see themselves in relation to technology. 
 That shift is what The Garage is for. 
 Want to Experience It Yourself? 
 The physical AI space is open at the SAP headquarters in Walldorf , and we'd love to show you around. Whether you're curious about vibe coding, want to explore what Joule could mean for your day-to-day work, or simply want to see what innovation looks and feels like when it's hands-on, The Garage is the place to find out. 
 Get in touch to book a visit or learn more: experiencegarage@sap.com 
 Come for the machines. Leave with a new perspective.

title: LO-VC or AVC? How to Think About Variant Configuration in SAP S/4HANA
author: ashish_kakade
text:
The Meeting Where Everyone Pretends to Agree 
 Picture a room where the project lead is gesturing at a migration timeline, the configurator in the corner is quietly calculating how long it would take to rewrite three thousand dependencies, and the IT manager is nodding at a slide that reads "AVC is SAP's strategic direction" while privately thinking: strategic for whom, exactly, and by when? If you have sat in that room — or run that meeting — this post is for you. 
 The question of LO-VC versus AVC is one of the most practically important questions in SAP variant configuration right now, and it is also one of the most tangled. Let us untangle it, without the bullet points. 
 Two Engines, One Job (Sort Of) 
 Think of LO-VC and AVC the way you might think of two professional chefs. The first trained in classical French technique, has been in the kitchen for thirty years, and can cook anything — but insists on doing things the old way and is not picking up any new recipes. The second trained on modern cuisine, works with precision instruments, and has an open calendar for whatever comes next. Both can feed you dinner. Only one of them is still learning new dishes. 
 LO-VC — Logistics Variant Configuration — is the legacy engine that has powered product configuration in SAP ERP since the 1990s. It sits deep in the ABAP stack, is tightly woven into business processes, and has been battle-tested across practically every manufacturing industry imaginable — from automotive and industrial machinery to high-tech electronics and engineered-to-order equipment. It is mature, stable, and still fully supported. 
 AVC — Advanced Variant Configuration — is the next-generation successor. It uses a constraint-based solver called Gecode — developed under the lead of Prof. Christian Schulte at KTH Royal Institute of Technology in Stockholm and extended by SAP in cooperation with the Fraunhofer Institute for Industrial Mathematics (ITWM) in Kaiserslautern, Germany. Gecode is an award-winning solver, and the performance difference is not marginal: AVC resolves complex configuration models significantly faster than the classic engine, with the advantage growing as model complexity increases. 
 It ships with modern Fiori applications, a dedicated simulation environment where you can test any configuration scenario before it touches a live order, embedded analytics at the characteristic level, and deep integration with SAP Commerce Cloud and SAP CPQ. 

 The Roadmap Message SAP Actually Means (Yes, Really) 
 There is one sentence from Dr. Petra Meyer, AVC Product Manager at SAP, that keeps appearing in every internal and customer-facing conversation about this topic: "No new functionality in LO-VC. The roadmap is empty. AVC is SAP's strategic solution." That is not corporate hedging — it is a statement of engineering intent. LO-VC will receive maintenance and security corrections. The feature set, however, is frozen permanently, by design. 
 This matters in ways that go beyond a slide. LO-VC is not available in S/4HANA Public Cloud Edition, full stop. If your organisation is on a path toward public cloud, LO-VC is simply not part of that future. AVC is available in both private and public cloud editions and receives new capabilities with every release — Engineer-to-Order enhancements, Lot Size of 1 manufacturing scenarios, OData V4 APIs for sales order processing, support for complex multi-level solution quotations, and connectivity to SAP Commerce Cloud and SAP CPQ are all on active delivery. In Q1 2025, SAP also simplified the AVC licensing model to a single SKU covering all users — no separate tiers, no additional licences needed for engineers building models. The SAP Road Map Explorer entry for AVC is expanding; the one for LO-VC is, as promised, empty. SAP Note 3073312 contains the authoritative feature-by-feature comparison if you want the forensic detail. 
 So When Does It Make Sense to Stay on LO-VC (For Now)? 
 Honesty requires acknowledging that migrating from LO-VC to AVC is not a weekend project. The two engines use genuinely different modelling paradigms. Where LO-VC relies on procedural preconditions and procedures — step-by-step instructions the system follows — AVC uses declarative constraints, which describe what must be true without prescribing how to get there. For a model with thousands of dependencies written in LO-VC syntax, that is not a copy-and-paste migration. It is a re-design exercise. 
 If your LO-VC landscape is stable, your team is not cloud-bound yet, and you have no immediate pressure from a public cloud adoption programme, there is a reasonable argument for continuing to run LO-VC while planning the migration thoughtfully. "Thoughtfully" is the operative word. The window for that thoughtful planning is narrowing, not widening. 
 Why the Gap Is Bigger Than It Looks 
 The gaps show up in three places. 
 For end users, AVC's constraint engine — powered by Gecode — aggressively eliminates infeasible options as you configure. In LO-VC, a misconfigured dependency can silently allow combinations that only fail downstream — at production order creation, at procurement, or at delivery. AVC eliminates that class of error by design: invalid combinations are excluded as early as possible, so they rarely appear as choices at all. When a sales rep needs to change a value that has already been set, AVC lets them select an alternative without deleting the existing valuation. Filtering, undo, redo, and colour-coded tab guidance showing exactly where input is still needed round out a user experience that LO-VC's SAP GUI simply cannot match. 
 Before any of this reaches a live order, AVC also provides a dedicated Simulate Configuration Models app: a Fiori environment where you can test any product configuration scenario in a completely risk-free way. Run a full configuration, activate the dependency trace to see exactly which rules fired and why, inspect the resulting BOM, and understand why certain options appeared or disappeared — all without touching live data. This is as useful for sales training and customer demonstrations as it is for model validation and development. 

 For the engineers who build and maintain these models, AVC removes entire categories of workaround. Tasks that required multi-step helper dependencies in LO-VC — type conversions, string handling, complex table lookups — are handled concisely in AVC constraint syntax. Variant tables in AVC are more expressive too: they support multiple values per cell, intervals, wildcards, and rules that define forbidden combinations — capabilities that in LO-VC require workaround structures that bloat models and slow them down. When something is not behaving as expected, AVC's tracing environment lets you step through individual rule executions, filter by characteristic, and see exactly which inputs produced which outputs — turning what was a half-day debugging exercise into a fifteen-minute one. 

 For the business, the advantages show up where they matter most: order accuracy and speed. 
 AVC is the only engine that supports switching from Configure-to-Order to Engineer-to-Order mid-process. If a customer's requirements go beyond what standard options can cover, the salesperson switches to Engineer-to-Order mode — and every value they have already entered is preserved. This matters most for manufacturers who build products to a single customer's specification with no stock held: the "lot size of 1" scenario that industrial machinery, specialised equipment, and custom engineering companies deal with every day. The AVC model starts with a super BOM containing every possible component. As the configuration is completed, the engine selects the right parts, eliminates the incompatible ones, and delivers a complete, accurate, ready-to-manufacture bill of materials for that one customer's product. No manual rework, no post-order corrections. 
 Beyond individual order accuracy, AVC's embedded analytics give you business intelligence that LO-VC simply cannot provide: which characteristic combinations appear most often in orders, which configurations drive the most revenue, where customers consistently hit dead ends in the configuration process. These insights live at the characteristic level, flow into SAP analytics without custom development, and give your product management and sales teams the data to make informed decisions about your variant portfolio. 
 What Migration Actually Involves (No Glossing Over) 

 SAP provides dedicated tooling to make the transition from LO-VC to AVC manageable. The starting point is Transition Workspaces (transaction VCH_L2A_WORKSPACES), where you group your existing classic configuration models into packages. Each workspace is defined by a configurable product and one of its configuration profiles, and any number of models can be grouped together for collective processing — giving you an aggregated view of transition progress across related models. 
 The actual work happens in the Transition Workbench (transaction VCH_L2A_WORKBENCH). The Workbench assesses each model for AVC compatibility, converts the dependencies it can handle automatically, flags what still needs manual attention, and lets you simulate the transition steps before committing anything to the live system. Once models have been adapted, the Compare Engines tool (VCH_L2A_COMPARISON) runs a side-by-side comparison of LO-VC and AVC results on the same order or material variant — so you can confirm both engines produce equivalent output before you cut over. 
 LO-VC and AVC coexist in the same system during migration — you migrate model by model, validate each one, and carry the landscape forward incrementally. What migration cannot do is eliminate the re-design work for complex dependency logic. For large, mature landscapes — such as those in industrial machinery where manufacturers have been running LO-VC since ECC days — the translation effort is the honest centre of the migration cost estimate. SAP's tooling has matured significantly, and partial automation is now possible. But sizing the remaining manual work accurately, early, is what separates a migration that lands on time from one that keeps getting pushed. 
 The Integration Story and Why It Matters 
 Once you are on AVC, the integration picture changes fundamentally. AVC integrates with SAP Commerce Cloud and SAP CPQ — what SAP describes as the ability to "model once and configure anywhere." The mechanism is a Knowledge Base: a packaged runtime copy of your product configuration rules that is replicated to external systems. A B2B or B2C customer configuring a product on your Commerce Cloud storefront works from exactly the same constraint rules as your internal sales team in S/4HANA. The same options are available, the same rules apply, and the resulting configuration flows back to create a correctly configured sales document. No duplicate model maintenance, no synchronisation overhead. 
 Sales Order processing is also exposed via OData V4 API, enabling external integrations, custom applications, and automation workflows to interact with AVC-configured orders in a standardised, modern way. 
 One practical note for organisations already on LO-VC and using SAP Commerce Cloud or SAP CPQ — or planning to: certain classic LO-VC variant table constructs are explicitly documented by SAP as incompatible with those external platforms. AVC variant tables do not have this limitation. Migration may already be relevant to integration challenges your team is dealing with today, not just a future-state consideration. 
 None of these integrations exist for LO-VC. If your business needs to configure products through a web channel or connect to an external quoting tool, AVC is not just the better option — it is the only one on SAP's roadmap.

title: How to Automatically Determine the Confirmation Control Key in a PO Based on Storage Location
author: Leelamohan
text:
Introduction 
 In many implementations, one plant runs two kinds of storage locations. Some are managed by Warehouse Management (WM) and others only by Inventory Management (IM). Inbound processing differs between them. WM locations benefit from an Inbound Delivery, which lets the warehouse plan putaway before goods arrive. IM locations don’t need that step. 
 Buyers usually have to remember which locations need which confirmation setup. That is error-prone. This post shows how to make the Confirmation Control Key in the Purchase Order determine itself from the storage location, with no manual input. 
 Business Requirement 
 Storage Location Type Expected behavior in PO 
 WM - Managed Lcoation Confirmation Control Key is determined automatically 
 IM - Managed Location Confirmation Control Key remains blank 
 The goal is to drive confirmation processing dynamically from the storage location on the PO item. 
 Solution Overview 
 The solution uses standard configuration in Logistics Execution, where the confirmation control is assigned per combination of PO category, document type, plant and storage location. 
 If the PO item's storage location has an entry (wm location), the key is proposed automatically. 
 If there is no entry, as for IM locations, the keys remains blank. 
 No enhancement or custom code is needed. 
 Step-by-Step Configuration 
 Step 1: Open the Configuration node 
 Go to SPRO --> SAP Reference IMG --> Logistics Execution --> Shipping --> Deliveries --> Define Order Confirmations for Inbound Deliveries 

 Step 2: Create the determination entries 
 Choose New Entries and maintain one entry for each WM-managed storage location: 
 Field Value Description 
 Category F Purchase Order 
 Order Type PO Document type (e.g. NB) The PO document type in scope 
 Plant Plant code The plant of the WM location 
 Storage Location Location code The WM managed storage location 
 Confirmation Control 0004 Inbound Delivery 
 Testing the Result 
 Scenario 1: PO with IM-Managed storage location 
 Go to ME21N and create a PO with the relevant document type 
 Enter the item with the plant and the IM managed storage location 
 Open the item's confirmation tab 
 Result: The confirmation Control key is Blank. 

 Scenario 2: PO with WM-Managed storage location 
 Go to ME21N and create a PO with the relevant document type 
 Enter the item with the plant and the IM managed storage location 
 Open the item's confirmation tab 
 Result: The confirmation Control key is determined automatically as 0004 (inbound Delivery) 

 Benefits: 
 Fewer manual erros - Buyers no longer have to know which locations need which key. 
 Consistent Procss - Every PO to a WM location is set up for inbound delivery. 
 Better warehouse planning - Putaway can be prepared before goods receipt. 

 If you found this guide helpful, don't miss any other SAP MM WM EWM blogs covering real-world automation, configurations tips, and best practices for procurement, inventory management, and warehouse management.

 Mannem Leelamohan

title: From AI to Analytics: Where SAP Fieldglass Stands Out in the 2026 SIA VMS Landscape
author: Ansley Condon
text:
The external workforce has become an essential part of how organizations access specialized skills, respond to changing business needs, and stay flexible. And as external talent plays a bigger role in workforce strategy, the technology used to manage it must evolve, too. 

 Staffing Industry Analysts’ 2026 Vendor Management Systems (VMS) Landscape illustrates just how far VMS platforms have come and where they are heading next. 

 Adoption is already widespread. According to SIA, 88% of surveyed organizations in the Americas and 86% in Europe use a VMS, while another 12% in each region are likely to explore implementation over the next two years. Global VMS spend under management reached US$303 billion in 2025, up 7% year over year. 
 Get an objective, data-driven view of how SAP Fieldglass performs across contingent workforce management, SOW, compliance, and AI 

 Download the SIA report 

 But what stands out from these figures is how much more organizations now expect from these platforms. SIA describes VMS platforms as moving beyond systems of record to become strategic workforce platforms, taking on a broader role in process automation, compliance and risk management, advanced analytics, and data-driven decision-making. 

 For workforce leaders, the next era of external workforce management will be defined not just by transactional efficiency, but by how effectively organizations can connect technology, data, and intelligence to make better workforce and spend decisions. 

 Connected data becomes the foundation 

 As external workforce programs grow more sophisticated, businesses need a clearer view of the people, suppliers, skills, services, and spend supporting their operations. 

 SIA emphasizes that accurate and well-governed external workforce data is increasingly important for reporting, predictive analytics, workforce intelligence, and AI. Organizations looking to get more value from AI must first prioritize a strong data foundation. Fragmented or incomplete information can limit the quality of the recommendations and insights AI provides. 

 The SIA findings are encouraging for SAP Fieldglass in this area. The report gives SAP Fieldglass a 4.93 out of 5 score for reporting and analytics, with capabilities across workforce analytics, supplier performance, SOW visibility, and workforce planning. 

 When data is connected and accessible, VMS platforms can do more than show leaders what has already happened. It can help them identify patterns, anticipate what may happen next, and make more informed decisions about workforce strategy. That is when workforce data becomes a strategic asset rather than simply a system record. 

 Services procurement moves closer to the center 

 SIA identifies the growing importance of services procurement, with statement-of-work management as a strategic priority for both VMS buyers and providers. The field guide notes that SOW represents 39% of spend, while only 13% of client programs currently manage SOW within their VMS platform. 

 That gap points to a significant opportunity. Services represent a substantial share of external spend, yet many organizations still manage that spend outside the VMS. 

 Companies increasingly rely on external providers for much more than individual workers. They bring in specialized expertise, project teams, and service providers to deliver defined outcomes. Managing those relationships requires more visibility into suppliers, budgets, milestones, deliverables, compliance, and performance. 

 In the SIA assessment, SAP Fieldglass scores 4.96 for SOW and services procurement. But the broader takeaway is that external workforce management can no longer treat workers and services as entirely separate areas. As services become a larger and more strategic part of external spend, organizations need a more connected way to manage both and understand how they contribute to business outcomes. 

 Global scale is really about managing complexity 

 Managing an external workforce across multiple countries is about much more than geographic reach. Every market can bring a different mix of labor classifications, tax requirements, supplier structures, regulations, and operating models. 

 Global scale should therefore be measured by more than the number of countries a platform can support. The real challenge is creating consistency while retaining the flexibility to address local requirements. 

 SAP Fieldglass earned top scores in areas including supplier and engagement management, compliance and audit, and mobile enablement. The field guide also identifies SAP Fieldglass as the leader in geographic coverage and notes support for more than 190 countries and 21 languages. 

 For global businesses, capabilities such as worker classification validation, supplier qualification workflows, and configurable onboarding requirements can help create a common framework across markets while accounting for local requirements. The real measure of global scale isn’t simply where a VMS operates. It’s how consistently it can help organizations manage workforce complexity across those markets. 

 AI moves from assistance toward intelligence and action 

 AI is another area where the market is moving quickly, with an important reality check. 

 SIA finds that while VMS AI is expanding into areas such as AI agents, predictive analytics, and candidate assessment, adoption remains measured. Buyers are also looking for transparency, configurability, human oversight, and clearer evidence of business value. 

 That balance matters. The most useful question isn’t simply how many capabilities a platform offers, but how that AI works in practice. Is it grounded in trusted workforce data? Is it built into the workflows where decisions are already happening? Can it help people act in ways that are useful, explainable, and governed? 

 SAP Fieldglass received the second-highest embedded AI assessment in the field guide’s overall summary, driven by capabilities designed to connect data, intelligence, and automation across workforce and procurement processes. 

 The meaningful shift isn’t simply toward more AI. It’s from AI that assists with individual tasks to intelligence that helps inform decisions and, with appropriate oversight, enables action. 

 That evolution is likely to accelerate. But more AI does not automatically mean more value. Lasting impact will depend on pairing sophisticated AI with the right data foundation, strong governance, and connectivity across the enterprise. 

 The VMS of the future is a decision platform 

 SAP Fieldglass received the second-highest overall capability score in the SIA landscape, with particularly strong performance across supplier management, services procurement, analytics, compliance, and mobile enablement. But the bigger story goes beyond any score. 

 External workforce management is becoming more connected. Leaders need to understand people alongside services, suppliers, skills, spend, and risk. They need workforce data that can move across business processes rather than sit in isolated systems and intelligence that helps turn that information into better, faster decisions. 

 The organizations best prepared for what comes next will be those that can bring those pieces together to build a more agile, informed, and resilient external workforce strategy. 

 That is where the next generation of VMS technology is heading. 

 Ansley Condon is global GTM lead for SAP Fieldglass.

title: Dutch Ministry of Defense Chooses SAP Sovereign Cloud: A Milestone for European Defense Readiness
author: Martin Merz
text:
Digital sovereignty is essential to Europe’s defense readiness. It gives armed forces the freedom to act, the ability to adapt, and the confidence to embrace new technologies. 

 That is why SAP and the Dutch Ministry of Defense have signed a strategic agreement to develop and manage a sovereign cloud environment in the Netherlands. This marks a significant milestone for SAP Sovereign Cloud in the European Defense Sector. It enables the Dutch armed forces to modernize critical digital systems while strengthening security, improving resilience, and creating the foundation for future cloud and AI innovation. 
 Handle critical data confidently with the control, resilience, and compliance your business requires 

 Learn more 

 Reliable and innovative digital systems are increasingly essential to defense readiness, with recent conflicts demonstrating the importance of cloud resilience. The cloud environment in this case will be designed around the Ministry of Defense’s specific security and sovereignty requirements, with SAP responsible for maintenance, updates, and key aspects of operations. It is scheduled to become operational on January 1, 2028. 

 As Thomas Saueressig, Chief Customer Officer and member of the Executive Board of SAP SE, emphasizes, the key is to bring innovation and sovereignty together: “For the Dutch Ministry of Defense, it is essential to benefit from modern technology while retaining control over the security and sovereignty of its critical digital systems. This partnership demonstrates how these priorities can go hand in hand. As a European technology company, we are supporting the Ministry of Defense in its ongoing digital transformation with a cloud environment that meets its specific security and sovereignty requirements.” 

 Greater resilience through a multicloud strategy 

 SAP Sovereign Cloud will form part of the Ministry of Defense’s broader multicloud strategy, which combines different cloud environments based on the security and operational requirements of individual applications. This includes sovereign cloud, private cloud, and environments for highly classified information. 

 By diversifying its cloud infrastructure, Dutch Defense aims to reduce dependencies on individual technologies and providers while strengthening its ability to maintain and restore critical services during disruptions, including cyberattacks. 

 Bart Van der Biest, managing director SAP Benelux, highlights why that ability to retain control matters over the longer term: “With a sovereign cloud, it is not just about where data is stored, but also about who has access to systems and who runs cloud operations. Those decisions must remain in the hands of the Ministry of Defense, regardless of how technology or geopolitics change. Ultimately, sovereignty is not only about the control you have today, but also about the freedom you retain tomorrow.” 

 From national milestone to European role model 

 This agreement provides a foundation for expanding sovereign cloud capabilities as Dutch Defense’s technological and operational needs evolve. It could serve as a basis for other eligible Dutch government entities seeking to modernize critical services under comparable security and sovereignty requirements. 

 Further, with this agreement, the Dutch Ministry of Defense is demonstrating how digital sovereignty can move from strategic ambition into practical implementation. Across Europe, armed forces and security-sensitive organizations face the same challenge: modernizing critical systems, embracing innovation, and building long-term resilience. Sovereign cloud provides a foundation to help achieve these goals. 

 The Netherlands is setting an important example for Europe: digital sovereignty becomes meaningful when it translates into real capabilities, greater resilience, and the freedom to share the future with confidence. 

 Martin Merz is president of SAP Sovereign Cloud.
